Ilorin Innovation Hub · ORBIT

Running ORBIT — Admin

Everything this role can reach, and nothing it cannot. ORBIT now runs itself: the ORBIT Agent admits applicants, marks work, reviews logbooks and writes each week's tasks. This is how that works, what staff can still do, and every screen you would use to do it.

For Admins Platform orbit2.iih.ng Cohort ORBIT 2.0

Before the first letter goes out: set the signatory, in Admin → Settings → General Settings. Until a super admin saves one, every acceptance letter prints with a blank signature line. It takes about thirty seconds — Section 04 has the steps.

ORBIT is where an application becomes an intern: the public form feeds a queue, the queue produces a decision, the decision produces a letter the applicant's university needs, and everything after that — placement, tasks, logbooks, sign-off — hangs off the same record.

Since 29 September 2026 nobody has to operate it. The ORBIT Agent does the work staff used to do, and timers make sure nothing waits on a person (Section 01). Every staff screen still works, so this manual is for looking up how something works or stepping in by choice — not a list of chores. It is written to be looked up rather than read through, so each section stands on its own.

Section 01

How ORBIT runs itself

Every job that used to need a member of staff is now done by the ORBIT Agent — an automated assistant with its own account (orbit.agent@iih.ng), so every decision it makes is recorded under its name, never yours.

JobWhat the agent doesIf it cannot decide
AdmissionsTwo independent models screen each application; if they agree it is genuine, the agent approves it and places the applicant in the least-busy stream of their first-choice track. Acceptance email (and SIWES letter) follow automatically.A split verdict is admitted after 3 days; an application nobody screened, after 7. Two screeners agreeing on spam or ineligible keeps it out.
MarkingTwo models read each submission — text, files, links — and must agree on a score; a third breaks ties. A unanimous zero (usually work for the wrong task) goes back to the intern to redo.Work it cannot open or agree on is approved at full points 5 days after it was set aside, with feedback saying it was not individually assessed. Anything at all is settled after 14 days.
LogbooksDaily logs are reviewed by two models; one is returned only if both say it describes no real work. Weeks are signed off once they end, have an approved log and nothing is waiting.Split reviews are approved after 5 days; anything after 14.
TasksEach week, for every stream with nothing live, the agent writes fresh tasks and a second model vets each for safety and whether it can be marked. Survivors publish straight away and interns get one message per stream.On Saturdays the prepared task bank tops up any stream the agent missed.
CohortsThree weeks before a cohort ends, the next one is opened as a draft; it becomes active on its start date and the old one closes once it has.—
QuestionsInterns who message the ORBIT Agent get a reply grounded in how ORBIT actually works and in their own record.A reply that fails its check is replaced by a short, safe one.

The timers are the safety net. The agent's reading runs on a machine outside ORBIT three times a day; the rules and timers run inside ORBIT itself. If that machine is off, work is delayed — never stranded, and never left for someone to notice.

What staff can still do

Everything. Staff screens are unchanged, and a person acting first always wins: a submission you review is never touched by the agent, an application you approve is simply approved, and a daily log you sign off is done. The agent only ever picks up what is still waiting.

Telling who decided

  • A submission the agent marked carries feedback ending “Assessed by ORBIT Agent …”; one settled by the timer says it was not individually assessed.
  • An application, daily log or weekly sign-off the agent decided names the ORBIT Agent as its reviewer.
  • Tasks the agent wrote list the ORBIT Agent as their author.
Section 02

Signing in and what you can see

Everyone works from the same address — orbit2.iih.ng — and what you can reach is decided by your role. If a screen described here is missing, your account almost certainly does not carry the role for it; that is a permissions question for a super admin, not a fault.

The four roles

RoleReachesTypical holder
Super adminEverything, plus bulk import and role changesProgramme lead
AdminAdmissions, approvals, letters, placement, streams, tasks, usersProgramme staff
Moderator (supervisor)Their own streams, their interns’ submissions and logbooksTeam leads supervising interns
InternTheir own tasks, submissions, logbook and profileThe students on placement

A moderator only ever sees the streams they moderate. This is enforced on the server, not by hiding buttons — so a supervisor cannot reach another team’s submissions by any route.

Finding your way around

When something is wrong

There is a Report a bug button on every page, bottom right. It takes one sentence and records which screen you were on, which is the part people usually cannot remember later. It works signed out too — useful when the thing that is broken is the sign-in page itself. Anywhere this manual says to raise something, that is the channel.

Do not paste a password or a sign-in link into a bug report. The page address is attached automatically, with anything sensitive stripped out of it.

The green Admin button in the top bar opens the staff area. Inside it, the row of tabs — Overview, Streams, Tasks, Users, Applications, SIWES, Gamification, Settings — is most of the administrative platform, but not all of it. Three things staff use daily sit OUTSIDE it, on the main navigation: Manual (this document, in the app, with a PDF to download), the review dashboard, and the task proposal queue.

Section 03

Admissions: reading and approving applications

Applications arrive from the public form at orbit2.iih.ng/apply. Nobody needs an account to apply, and nothing you do in ORBIT sends the form out — it is simply always open.

You do not need to approve anyone. The ORBIT Agent screens every new application within hours and approves genuine ones itself (Section 01). The steps below are for when you want to decide one yourself — an application you approve is simply approved, and the agent leaves it alone.

Opening the queue

  1. Click Admin in the top bar.
  2. Open the Applications tab — this is the queue for all four programmes.
  3. (SIWES → Applications shows the same screen filtered to SIWES only.)

Getting the data out

Export to Excel, on the Applications screen, downloads every application as a workbook — the same columns the old Google Sheet carried. It is generated when you press it, so it is current, and it is a snapshot: the file is dated, and it does not update itself afterwards.

The Google Sheet is disconnected. It no longer receives applications and it no longer approves anyone — a Status column edited there does nothing. If you have it bookmarked, stop consulting it; it is frozen at the day it was switched off. Approval happens here — by the ORBIT Agent or an admin, and the record names which — and the export above replaces it for anything you used the sheet to read.

The export names each applicant's documents but never contains them. The passport photograph and the placement letter stay in ORBIT behind a sign-in. A downloaded workbook gets forwarded and copied like any other file, and an identity document inside one travels with it.

Four programmes, one queue

ORBIT is not a SIWES-only platform, and the queue is not a SIWES-only queue. Applicants choose SIWES, Internship, NYSC or Volunteer, and on the live platform SIWES is the minority — of the applications waiting now, roughly two in three are one of the other three.

The coloured badge beside each name is the programme. It matters because the rest of the row changes with it: a SIWES applicant supplies an institution, course, matric number and placement dates, and a volunteer supplies none of them. The Programme column shows what that person actually gave you rather than a row of dashes.

Only SIWES applicants receive an acceptance letter, and only SIWES interns keep a logbook. Everything else — tasks, submissions, points, streams, community — works the same for all four.

Reading a row

Each row carries everything a decision needs: the applicant and their contact details, their reference code, the institution, course, matric number and placement dates, and a link to the SIWES form or letter they uploaded.

Documents open through an authenticated link rather than a public URL, so the tab may take a moment. If nothing opens, your session has probably expired — sign in again and retry.

Approving

  1. Find the applicant. The search box matches name, email and reference code.
  2. Click Approve on their row.
  3. Read the name in the confirmation prompt, then confirm.

Approval cannot be undone. There is no route back to Submitted, which is why the prompt names the applicant rather than asking “are you sure” — reading the name is what catches the wrong row. An approved row stops offering an Approve button at all.

Approving several at once

Tick the checkboxes on the rows you want and use the bulk action above the table. Only rows still awaiting a decision can be selected — an approved application has nothing left to do to it. Changing the filter clears your selection, deliberately: a selection that survived a filter change would be a selection of rows you can no longer see.

Section 04

Acceptance letters

A university’s Industrial Liaison Unit will not accept a placement until it holds a letter from the host organisation confirming the student was taken. ORBIT generates that letter from the application, on IIH letterhead, with the wording fixed to the approved template.

First: set who signs

Do this once. Until it is set, every letter prints with a blank signature line and the screen will tell you the HR signatory is missing.

  1. Open Admin → Settings → General Settings.
  2. In Acceptance letter signatory, choose the person who signs and set their job title.
  3. Save. Every letter from then on uses it.

Super admin only, and not editable from the letter itself. The letter screen shows you who is set but cannot change it — deliberately: gating the stored value would mean nothing if the printed name were a free-text box beside the Print button. An admin can still print letters; they just cannot change whose name signs them — that is a super admin setting.

SIWES applicants only. An approved internship, NYSC or volunteer row shows no letter button, and a batch run passes over them. The letter is addressed to a university's Industrial Liaison Unit and titled “for SIWES placement” — an office a volunteer has no relationship with.

One letter

  1. In the Applications queue, set the status filter to Approved.
  2. Click Acceptance letter on the applicant’s row.
  3. Check the letter date, then click Print.
  4. In the print dialog choose Save as PDF, or print on plain paper — the IIH letterhead is part of the generated document, so pre-printed headed paper would print it twice.

Pronouns come from the gender the applicant gave on the form. Answered, the letter reads “She will undergo her industrial training”; left blank, it falls back to “He/She … his/her” rather than guessing on a document the university keeps.

The whole cohort at once

Acceptance letters at the top of the queue gathers every approved SIWES applicant — not just the ones on screen — and lays them out one per page for a single print run.

Read the warnings before you print

If an application is missing something the letter needs — no department, no level, no university, no signatory — the letter still prints, with that clause dropped so the sentence still reads as English. The amber panel above the letters is the only thing that tells you. A letter that quietly omits the department reads as complete and is not.

A missing field cannot be corrected from the approved application — the intake record is fixed once a decision is made, and there is no staff edit for it. What you CAN correct is the source the letter reads from: the signatory in Admin → Settings → General Settings, and the intern's department and cohort under SIWES → Interns. Fix those, then reprint. If the wrong value is one only the applicant supplied, raise it rather than reprinting around it — the letter and the intern's file are supposed to agree.

Reprinting

Letters are not stored. Each one is generated fresh from the application, so a letter that goes astray is reprinted by opening the row again — and a correction to the application shows up on the next print automatically.

Section 05

Placement and conversion

Approval says yes. Placement says how: whether the intern works on site, which stream they join, and who supervises them. When the ORBIT Agent admits someone it places them itself — in the least-busy stream of the first track they chose, in the current cohort (or the incoming one, in a cohort's last fortnight). Use Assign on the application row to decide a placement yourself before approving.

Automatic placement only works for streams that belong to a track. A new stream that is not attached to one is never chosen, so attach it when you create it.

What you set

FieldWhat it means
Participation modeVirtual (online), Hybrid (on site one day a week), or Physical (on site). SIWES placements are virtual for everyone, wherever the student lives — do not put a SIWES intern on site. For the other programmes, Ilorin-based interns are hybrid and attend on Mondays.
ReasonRequired when you override the mode the applicant asked for
On-site dayWhich weekday a hybrid intern attends. Monday, unless there is a specific reason — a cohort scattered across the week has no day when the Hub is full.
StreamThe team they join and receive tasks from
SupervisorThe person who reviews their work and signs their logbook

The reason field exists because a mode override is a decision someone will ask about later — usually the intern. Writing it down at the time is cheaper than reconstructing it.

Becoming an intern

Conversion is automatic and starts the moment you approve — an approved applicant becomes an intern account straight away, and appears under SIWES → Interns. A job every fifteen minutes retries anything that failed, so that interval is a safety net rather than the normal wait. There is no button to press, and approving twice does not make it faster.

Once converted, the intern is managed from the Interns register rather than the application row, which has done its job.

If someone approved more than fifteen minutes ago still has not appeared, the retry sweep has had a go and not succeeded — that is worth raising rather than re-approving — the record is already approved and the sweep will not create them twice.

Cohorts and departments

A cohort carries the programme dates and the logbook rules — which days need a daily log, when weekly summaries are due, whether sign-off is required. Departments are the IIH teams interns are attached to.

Section 06

Streams and tasks

A stream is a team with its own members, feed and work. Tasks are published into a stream, and only its members see them.

Every week the ORBIT Agent writes each stream's tasks. For any stream with no live task, it drafts five against the programme's rules — doable virtually, from public material, safe, and markable from the submission — has a second model vet each one, and publishes the survivors. They are priced by the same complexity rules as a task you write, and every intern in the stream gets one message listing them. You can still add tasks of your own at any time.

Creating a task

  1. Open Admin → Tasks and click Create Task. Admins only — a supervisor has no Admin button; supervisors shape the week by approving or editing proposals in the task queue instead.
  2. Choose the stream — a task with no stream reaches nobody.
  3. Write a title and full instructions.
  4. Check the deadline. It is pre-filled from the cohort’s weekly cadence; change it if this task differs.
  5. Set the points and how work should be submitted — text, link or file.
  6. Click Create Task.

Tasks cannot be created or assigned before the programme starts. If the Create Task button is disabled, check the cohort’s start date — the message on screen names it.

Active and inactive

Deactivating a task withdraws it without destroying submissions already made against it. That is almost always what you want instead of deleting.

Section 07

Reviewing submissions

Submitted work waits on the Review Submissions screen. Supervisors see their own streams; admins see everything.

The ORBIT Agent marks this queue for you, three times a day. What you see here is what it has not reached yet, or has set aside because it could not read the work or its markers disagreed. Reviewing one yourself is always allowed and always wins; the agent never touches a submission a person has decided.

How you get there depends on your role. Supervisors open the profile menu — your avatar, top right — and choose Review Submissions. There is no Admin button on a supervisor account and there is not meant to be; the review screens are reached from the profile menu instead. Admins can use either route.

Making a decision

  1. Filter by status, or search by intern, task or stream.
  2. Click the submission to open it.
  3. Choose Approve, Request Changes or Reject.
  4. For an approval, set the points to award. For anything else, write the feedback — it is required.
  5. Click Submit Review.
DecisionWhat happensPoints
ApproveWork accepted and closedAwarded, up to the task maximum
Request changesReturns to the intern, who can resubmitNone
RejectClosed without acceptanceNone

Feedback is mandatory for anything that is not an approval. An intern who is told only “changes requested” has been given a verdict, not a way forward.

A submission can be resubmitted after Request changes, but not after Approve or Reject — both are final.

Section 08

Logbook and attendance sign-off

SIWES requires a logbook the university will inspect, so this is the part with an external deadline. The Review Dashboard collects everything waiting on a supervisor.

The ORBIT Agent reviews daily logs and signs off weeks, so this dashboard is no longer a to-do list. A log is sent back only when two independent reviewers agree it describes no real work; a week is signed off once it has ended, has at least one approved log, and nothing in it is waiting or was sent back. The sign-off names the ORBIT Agent. You can still review anything that is waiting.

TabWhat is in it
Pending logsDaily logs submitted and waiting to be reviewed
Sign-offsWeekly summaries awaiting a supervisor’s sign-off
My internsThe people you supervise
Missing logsDays that should have a log and do not
AttendanceCheck-ins that need attention — absences and exceptions

Who keeps a logbook

SIWES interns, and nobody else. The logbook exists to be inspected by a university's Industrial Liaison Unit; an internship, NYSC or volunteer participant has no institution expecting one, so ORBIT does not ask them for one, does not remind them about one, and does not count them as missing one on this dashboard.

This is decided by the programme on the person's record. An account created by hand or by import carries no programme, so if a SIWES intern is missing their logbook tabs, that is the field to check first.

Reviewing a log

  1. Open the profile menu (your avatar, top right) and choose Review Logbooks.
  2. On Pending logs, click Review on an entry.
  3. Read the work described, then approve it or send it back with a comment.

Missing logs is the number that matters at the end of the placement. A gap is far easier to resolve in the week it happens than in the month the university asks for the completed logbook.

Verification writes against the intern’s record, not the supervisor’s, so a supervisor signing off work never affects their own logbook.

Section 09

Users, accounts and settings

Admin → Users is the account register: create accounts, edit them, change roles, deactivate, and export the list you are looking at.

Deactivating rather than deleting

Deactivating blocks sign-in and keeps everything the person did. It is reversible. Use it when someone leaves the programme.

Deleting moves an account to trash, from which it can be restored. Delete forever is exactly that, and only a SUPER ADMIN can do it — an ordinary admin will not see the option, which is a permission boundary and not a fault. Prefer deactivation unless the account was created in error.

Adding people

  • One at a time — Add User creates an account and can send them a password.
  • In bulk — import a CSV or spreadsheet. Super admin only. Re-importing the same file does not create duplicates.
  • From an application — the normal route for interns, covered in Section 05.

Who has actually signed in

The register carries a Last sign-in column and a filter for it. An account that has never been used shows Never. In the first week of a cohort this is the number that matters: signing in is the first thing every new intern has to do, and this is how you see who has.

Signing in is not the only thing, though. The home page shows a new member a short Your first steps checklist — sign in, set a password, read the orientation manual — and it disappears once they finish. The password step is the one worth chasing: sign-in links expire, and a member without a password needs a new email every time they come back.

Set the filter to Never signed in for the list of people to chase. If that list is not shrinking, check whether outgoing mail is held (Section 11) before assuming the accounts are at fault.

Settings worth knowing

  • Email logs — every message ORBIT tried to send, and what happened to it. Sent means ORBIT handed it to the mail service, not that it reached an inbox. Check here first when someone says they never received a mail; Section 11 covers this in full.
  • Gamification — levels and badges, and the points thresholds between them.
  • Backup management — exports of platform data.

Roles take effect immediately on the server — every permission is re-checked on each request, so a demotion bites on the demoted person’s very next action. What can lag is their own screen: the navigation they are looking at was drawn with their old roles. If someone was just promoted and still cannot see a screen, a reload is enough; they do not need to sign out.

Section 10

Task proposals: work the agent drafts

The proposal queue matters far less than it used to. The ORBIT Agent now publishes each week's tasks itself, after a second model has vetted them (Section 06), so its tasks no longer wait here. What still arrives as a proposal:

  • The Saturday top-up from the prepared task bank, for any stream the agent did not write for that week.
  • Tasks a person creates through the agent’s connection rather than in the browser.

Proposals publish themselves

A proposal nobody answers publishes itself once the approval window passes (48 hours), with no approver recorded. That keeps a quiet week from becoming a week with no work in it — so an unattended queue is not a problem to solve. You can still step in:

  1. Open Tasks, then Task proposals.
  2. Read the draft — stream, deadline, points and how work should be submitted.
  3. Choose Approve and publish, Edit first if it needs changing, or Decline.
  4. A decline asks for a reason. Write one — it is the only record that survives.

Declining deletes the proposal. There is no declined list and no recycle bin — only your reason, in the audit log. If the task is salvageable, use Edit first instead.

Request another task, above the list, drafts the next prepared task for a stream as a new proposal — useful after a decline.

Section 11

Email: logs, holds, and why nothing arrived

Almost every complaint that reaches you as “the account is broken” is really a mail question: the sign-in link never arrived. This section is where to look, in order.

First: is mail flowing at all?

ORBIT has two independent brakes on outgoing mail, and either one holds everything — notifications, acceptance letters, sign-in links, application receipts. Nothing is lost while a brake is on; messages queue up and send when it is released.

BRAKEWHERE IT LIVESWHO CAN RELEASE IT
The pause switchAdmin → Settings → General SettingsSuper admin, from the app
The deployment holdSet on the deployment itselfWhoever administers the deployment — not from the app

While mail is held, the Users screen says so. A standing notice appears at the top of Admin → Users, and the password-reset actions report that a link was queued rather than sent. If you see that notice, no amount of resending will deliver anything — release the brake first.

Then: did this particular message go?

Reach it from Admin → Settings → Email Configuration → View Email Logs. Search by the person’s address. Open any row to see its delivery attempts — every try, when it happened, how long the provider took, and the exact error. Three failures for three different reasons look nothing like three for one, and only the attempt history tells them apart.

  • No row at all — the message was never queued. The action that should have created it did not run; check you completed it.
  • Pending — waiting. Either for the next run, or out a retry backoff after a failed attempt; the row shows when the next try is due. A brake being on is the usual reason nothing moves at all.
  • Sending — a drain run holds it right now. Leave it; it resolves within a few minutes.
  • Cancelled — someone stopped it deliberately. NOT a failure, and never retried on its own. Requeue it if that was a mistake.
  • Failed — attempted and refused. The reason on the row is the actual error from the mail service.
  • Sent — ORBIT handed it over successfully. If the recipient still has nothing, it is in their spam folder or their institution blocked it.

A message body IS kept, but reading one is deliberately awkward: only a super admin can, it is written to the audit log naming who looked, and there is no bulk view. That is because a sign-in email contains a live credential — opening one is closer to borrowing someone’s account than to reading a log.

Acting on a message

Two actions sit on each row, and they appear only where they would work — the server refuses the rest, so a button that is not offered is not a permissions problem.

  • Requeue — puts a failed or cancelled message back in the queue and clears its retry count, so it starts again from a clean slate. Use it after fixing whatever caused the failure. It is audited, because requeuing an unexpired sign-in email re-delivers a live credential to somebody’s mailbox on your say-so.
  • Stop — cancels a message that has not gone out. The recipient will not get it and nothing else in the system will notice, so it asks first. Requeue afterwards if you stopped it in error.

Neither is offered for a message already sent, or for one a run is holding right now — that send may already be in flight, and marking it otherwise would leave the log asserting something that did not happen.

Reading the queue at a glance

Above the log is a summary that separates the three ways a message can sit unsent, because they look identical in a status column and need different responses: waiting to send (nothing to do), retrying (backing off after a failure — also nothing to do, it is scheduled), and held because dispatch is paused, which is waiting on a person. During a hold, “18 pending” does not mean a queue about to move.

The panel can only see ONE of the two brakes. The pause switch lives in the database and is shown; the deployment hold is an environment variable that no screen can read. If messages stay pending while dispatch reads as running, that is the one to check — the screen says as much rather than guessing.

Week one: getting everyone signed in

New interns have no password. Conversion deliberately does not set one — they sign in with a magic link they request themselves, and a magic link is an email. So while mail is held, nobody can get in, and week one's only task cannot start. This is the sequence to open it.

  1. Confirm the accounts exist first: Admin → Users, filter Never signed in. Everyone you approved should be listed.
  2. Only if mail is actually held — a notice appears at the top of Admin → Users when it is — release it in Admin → Settings → General Settings. Super admin only. Mail sends normally by default, so on most cohorts there is nothing to release and this step is skipped.
  3. Watch the queued backlog drain in Email logs — rows move from Pending to Sent. This includes anything queued while the hold was on, so expect more than just today’s messages.
  4. Give it a few minutes, then reload the Users register. Names should start dropping off the Never signed in filter.
  5. For anyone still on that list after a day, select them and use the bulk sign-in-link action, then check Email logs for their address.

Releasing the hold sends everything waiting behind it, immediately. If the queue has been held for a while and you are not sure how old the backlog is, look at Email logs BEFORE releasing — those messages go to real applicants the moment you do.

An intern who says the link never arrived: check Email logs first. Sent means ORBIT handed it over and the problem is their inbox or their institution’s filter. Anything else is ours.

Section 12

Settings

One screen, at Admin → Settings, holding the things that change how the whole platform behaves rather than anything about one person.

  • General Settings — branding, and the two super-admin-only controls that matter most here: the outgoing email pause switch and the acceptance letter signatory.
  • Email configuration — the sending account, and the route through to the email logs.
  • Sign-in — the Zoho single-sign-on connection used by staff accounts.

Changes here apply to everyone at once and some of them are not visibly reversible from the same screen. Read what a control says before changing it, and if a setting mentions a deployment variable, it cannot be changed from the app at all.

Section 13

Keeping an eye on the agent

Nothing here needs doing on a schedule. It is where to look if something seems off, and what each signal means.

Where its work shows up

  • Audit log — every decision is written under the ORBIT Agent with an agent. action: agent.application_admitted, agent.tasks_published, agent.cohort_created, and so on.
  • Email logs (Section 11) — acceptances, marks, task messages and replies go out like any other mail, so a quiet week there is the first sign something has stopped.
  • Review Submissions — a queue that keeps growing for more than a couple of days means marking is not keeping up.

The machine that does the reading

The models that read applications, submissions, logs and messages run on a machine outside ORBIT, three times a day, using ORBIT's own subscriptions. It keeps its logs in ~/.openclaw/workspace/logs/orbit-agent/ and raises two flags there:

FileMeansUsually
UNHEALTHYA whole cycle failed on the agent’s sideA model sign-in has expired or a usage allowance ran out
BACKUP_FAILEDThe weekly backup could not be taken or verifiedLow disk space, or disk encryption switched off

If that machine is off, ORBIT does not stop: the timers inside ORBIT settle whatever is waiting — marks within 14 days at most, admissions within a week, logbooks within 14 days — and the prepared task bank tops up streams on Saturdays. Work is slower and less individually judged until it is back.

Backups

A copy of ORBIT's data (not uploaded files) is taken weekly on the same machine and checked before it is kept; the newest four are kept. It contains personal data and live sign-in sessions, so it stays on an encrypted disk, readable by its owner only, and out of Time Machine.

Screenshots are from the ORBIT test environment, so every name and record in them is fictional. The live platform looks identical.
